subject: Accounting
title: Corporate Income Tax
description: Learn Corporate Income Tax in one minute.

hook.text: Corporations are taxed on their profits—but the effective rate is often far below the headline rate.

buildup.text: The U.S. federal corporate tax rate is 21%. But deductions, credits, and loopholes slash the real bill.

discovery.text: Some profitable Fortune 500 companies pay zero federal tax in certain years.

twist.text: This isn't illegal—it's the result of tax incentives designed by lawmakers themselves.

climax.text: The gap between statutory and effective rates fuels endless debate about tax fairness.

punchline.text: The rate on paper and the rate they pay are not the same.

quiz.question: Why do some profitable companies pay zero corporate tax?
options: Legal deductions, credits, and incentives reduce their bill

details.summary: Corporate income tax is levied on business profits after deducting allowable expenses from revenue. It is one of the most debated taxes because of its impact on business investment, job creation, and international competitiveness.
details.whyItMatters: Corporate tax policy directly affects where companies invest, how they structure operations, and how much revenue governments collect, making it central to economic policy debates worldwide.
takeaways: Corporate tax is assessed on net profits — revenue minus allowable business expenses and deductions
U.S. corporate tax rate was reduced from 35% to 21% by the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act
Companies legally minimize corporate tax through deductions, credits, and strategic entity structuring

faq.question: How is corporate income tax calculated?
faq.answer: Corporations calculate taxable income by subtracting allowable expenses — salaries, rent, supplies, depreciation, interest — from total revenue. The applicable tax rate is then applied to this net profit figure. Various credits and incentives can further reduce the actual tax paid.

faq.question: Why is corporate tax so controversial?
faq.answer: Critics argue high rates drive businesses overseas and reduce investment; proponents say corporations should pay fairly for public infrastructure. The debate also involves whether corporate tax is ultimately borne by shareholders, employees, or consumers through higher prices.
